title: Tennis scoring explained: love, deuce and advantage

sources.name: USTA — Scoring points and tennis sets

sections.title: Love, 15, 30, 40: the first four scores
sections.html:
In tennis, love means zero; 15, 30 and 40 mean one, two and three points won in a game. Points build games, games build sets, and sets decide the match.

Call the server’s score first. At 30–40, the server has won two points and the receiver three. If the receiver wins the next rally, they win the game. If the server wins, the score becomes deuce.

The USTA scoring guide explains those unfamiliar numbers. Nobody has secretly won forty rallies.

sections.title: What comes after deuce?
sections.html:
Deuce is a tie at 40–40. Under advantage scoring, a player then needs two points in a row:

  1. Win the next point: advantage.
  2. Win again: game. Lose instead: back to deuce.

So winning one rally from deuce does not finish the game. Some matches use no-ad scoring, where one deciding point settles it instead. The LTA describes both formats.

sections.title: Read the scoreboard in layers
sections.html:
Keep the current game’s points separate from the set’s games. A player can lead 4–3 in games while trailing 30–40 in the current game.

In a usual tie-break set, 6–6 in games triggers a tie-break. That uses ordinary numbers, 1, 2, 3… A standard seven-point tie-break still needs a two-point lead; other formats exist.

sections.title: Try following one game
sections.html: Watch who serves, then follow the points until that game ends. Add sets once those numbers feel familiar. Next, find out when the players swap ends.

description: What do love, 30–40 and deuce mean? Follow tennis points, advantage and tie-breaks with one simple example, then read a scoreboard without guessing.
